meta: Dramas like Youth of May: Korean history that is not softened, and doomed romances that earn their endings.
standfirst: Gwangju, May 1980, and the history is not softened. This is not a romance with a sad ending, it is the Uprising with a love story inside it, and the framing device tells you early how this goes. The central death is abrupt and under-staged for the setup it was given, which is defensible and probably deliberate: nobody in Gwangju got a speech or a send-off. The side characters get no conclusions, and Lee Do Hyun is the breakout the show is remembered for. Do not start it looking for comfort, and do not start it expecting the ending to be earned in the usual way.

picks.why: History as the thing that separates two people, not a backdrop for their romance. Same structure of tenderness built carefully so the violence lands personally, same period detail treated as a moral obligation. Difference: twenty-one episodes on the Manchu invasions, so it is a full epic with a second half and a happy ending it has to fight for.

The same century seen from underneath, by people with no power in it. Same conviction that political history happens to specific families and the same refusal to let anyone be a symbol. Difference: it spans a life instead of one month, hope is the register, and the warmth is real, so it repairs where this one wounds.

The other great Korean drama about a country losing. Same doomed love inside a national catastrophe, same insistence on naming the year and the event. Difference: twenty-four hours, formal and operatic, and tragic all the way down, where this one gets twelve tight episodes of intimacy first.

A romance that history refuses to allow. Same shape of two people whose feelings are never the deciding factor, and the same restraint in how it is filmed. Difference: a palace instead of a massacre, no violence, and the obstacle is protocol rather than martial law, so it is a slow courtship at heavy 4.

Same writer, in the gentlest mode she has. Lee Kang again on people forced into roles they did not choose and the quiet lying that follows. Difference: contemporary, twins, and it resolves warmly, so the same instinct for buried pain arrives without the body count.

Tragedy signposted from the start and tenderness anyway. Same willingness to spend hours making you love people it intends to break, and the same use of a period setting as a trap. Difference: fantasy sageuk over twenty episodes at comfort 1, so the misery is longer and less specific than one documented month.

against.title: Snowdrop
against.why: The obvious pairing because it is the other 1980s political romance, and it is the one to skip. It puts a love story on top of the same decade with far less care about what actually happened, and the result is neither good history nor good melodrama.

against.title: Reply 1988
against.why: Recommended because of the era, and it is the cosy version of the same years. A street, families, jokes and a happy ending. Youth of May is about the state killing students in that same decade, and the tonal distance is total.

against.title: Chicago Typewriter
against.why: Paired for the history-plus-romance combination, and it treats the colonial period as a playful frame for a modern writer's block. Charming, and structurally the opposite of a show that refuses to let you look away from a date.
